video_title: Intel’s Optane Memory: A Promise Unfulfilled
transcript: In late July 2015, Intel and Micron  Technology announced what they called   the first new memory category in over 25 years. They dubbed it 3D XPoint.  And the two silicon giants   said that it could revolutionize  fast access to large sets of data. 3D XPoint is a nonvolatile memory like  NOR or NAND flash. So unlike DRAM,   it doesn't forget its data if the power goes out. There were big claims. It had read  and write speeds 1,000x faster than   NAND. And its endurance was 1,000x better. And it had up to ten times  the density of conventional   memory. A single individual die  can store 128 gigabits of data. 3D XPoint would evolve into the  Intel brand Optane. It promised   to be the next great memory. In today's video,   we take a look at Intel and Micron’s attempt  to introduce a whole new memory category. ## Beginnings DRAM and the flash memories are  charge-based memories - which means   that they store the bit in the form of electrons. Where they store that charge differs. The  flash memories store its electrons inside   a modified transistor's floating gate.  DRAM stores it inside a skinny capacitor. Phase Change Memories use a different physical   principle. They exploit a particular  material's ability to shift between   different phases. This material is called  (logically enough) a phase change material. When that material is in its crystalline  phase, its atoms are arranged in an orderly,   repeating pattern. So electricity flows through  easily - giving it a low resistivity value. Now if we melt the material down and quench it,  then the atoms take a new, amorphous phase -   basically a random arrangement kind of like glass.  Electricity cannot flow as easily through it,   making the resistivity far higher. This act of  switching to the amorphous phase is called RESET. How do we get the material back to a  crystalline phase? This act is known as   SET and it can be done with one of two ways.  The first being to melt it down to a liquid,   then slowly cooling the  melt until it crystallizes. The second is to directly turn the  amorphous solid into a crystal solid   by heating it to a temperature that is  high but not too high to melt. As you   might infer from this explanation, the SET  action is often the PCM's speed bottleneck. This heat can be generated in several  ways, depending on the cell's architecture.   A common architecture is the "mushroom  cell", where a cylindrical Joule heater   electrode comes in contact with a  film of the phase change material. The heater's shape spreads out  from the electrode - giving the   whole thing its mushroom-looking shape. The difference in resistivity  values between the crystalline   and amorphous phases can be quite  large - about three or four orders   in magnitude. So we can read the bit by  interrogating the material’s resistivity. The principles behind phase change  memory emerged in the late 1960s when   the legendary materials scientist  Stanford Ovshinsky discovered the   phase change behavior in a class of  materials called the chalcogenides. Such materials refer to compounds  with at least one chalcogen like   Tellurium alloyed with Germanium  or Antimony. Ovshinsky quickly   recognized that this behavior can  produce a semiconductor memory.   He and his firm Energy Conversion Devices  started working towards a prototype. ## Read-Mostly Memory In 1970, phase change memory technology  entered the market for the first time. RG Neale and DL Nelson of Energy  Conversion Devices and Gordon Moore   of Intel co-authored an article in  the venerable Electronics magazine   announcing what they called the  "Read-Mostly Memory" or RMM. RMM was pitched as a middle ground between RAM and  ROM. Back in the day, ROM referred to burned-in   memories that cannot be edited after production.  Since RAM is volatile and ROM is immutable,   RMM can store data that programs access often but  rarely edit - like lookup tables or something. Each RMM memory cell had a silicon  diode and a film of the phase-changing   material - branded the Ovionic material  after its discoverer Ovshinsky. Both sit   on a silicon substrate - which  helps make production simple. Energy Conversion Devices provided the  Ovionic material. Intel, the silicon   substrate. The cells were arranged  in a distinct and simple X-Y array. Unfortunately in 1970, people  could only produce cells with   a minimum feature size of about 10  micrometers. This rather large size   meant it took more power to switch them  - so these consumed quite a lot of power. The product also suffered relatively low speeds  - the crystallizing SET phase change took several   milliseconds - as well as low endurance.  At the same time, DRAM capacities scaled   up and new products like EPROMs entered  the market - and the RMM faded from view. Asked many years later about the article,   a then-79 year old Moore replied that  he did not recall it at all. Ouch. The product was tried one more time in  1978 by the computer-maker Burroughs   Corporation. Their team presented a phase  change memory device of about 1024-bits.   Unfortunately, the product suffered  critical reliability issues and was   not competitive. Things faded  from the mainstream for a bit. ## Ovonic Unified Memory Interest in chalcogenides renewed in the late  1990s when they were adopted for optical discs. Chalcogenide compounds were adopted for  rewritable CDs and DVDs. It was found that   these compounds' crystalline states were more  reflective than their amorphous ones. So a high   power laser inside the writer can program data  by heating the compounds on the disc surface. Moore's Law also triggered a re-evaluation  of the product. The programming current's   size scales down with the size of the  memory cell. The smaller the cell,   the smaller the current, and a  drastically less power-hungry memory. Soon, Ward Parkinson - a cofounder of  Micron Technology - and Tyler Lowrey - a   long-time CTO of Micron - saw these changes  and felt it was time to revisit PCM. In 1999,   they partnered with Ovshinsky's Energy  Conversion Devices to start Ovonyx. In February 2000, Ovonyx received a  big investment from Intel Capital,   as well as a licensing agreement. Then in 2001,  Intel started hyping Ovonic Unified Memory or OUM. Made with a 180 nanometer node, the OUM generated  heat with a resistor to do SET and RESET and had   a bipolar junction transistor to access data.  According to Lowrey, all you needed to do to   make it was to add a layer of the chalcogenide  material on top of a normal silicon semiconductor. Why was Intel so interested? At the  time, Intel was a dominant seller of   NOR flash - an older version of flash memory.  But NOR was hitting limits in scaling. The   memory cells had gotten so small that they  could no longer easily hold the charge. Intel presented OUM as a potential next step that   can replace only just flash  but also maybe DRAM and SRAM. The OUM product was then still in an  early research stage. It needed exotic,   expensive materials like tellurium, which drove up   the cost. And the strong currents needed  for SET and RESET were still rather large. However, Chipzilla's backing and  marketing muscle sparked renewed   interest in phase change memory in  both industry and academia. Samsung   and STMicroelectronics licensed Ovonyx's  technology and started their own PCM efforts. ## Numonyx In the end, the rise of another  type of flash memory called NAND   put the NOR flash business into secular decline. NAND packs memory cells far more  densely than NOR does. And it   pushed back flash memory's perceived  scaling limits. Its cheap cost-per-bit   got it specced into items like the iPod  and smartphones - eating away at NOR. In 2007, worldwide NOR flash sales fell 9%  year over year as NAND adoption by phones   accelerated. Continued declines  were expected in the years ahead.   NOR exposure was dragging down Intel's numbers. In 2008, Intel completed its spin off of  its NOR flash business by merging it with   STMicroelectronics' flash business to form a  new Switzerland-based company called Numonyx.   Numonyx also received a cash injection from the  PE firm Francisco Partners as well as a bank loan. So what was Numonyx going to do? The  NOR flash business was not the place   to be. NOR did not have NAND’s growth  prospects. NAND stores large pieces   of data and so had all the hard  disk drive storage market to eat. NOR on the other hand was more suited  for fast random reads - so stuff like   operating system code for embedded  devices. Not a growth market. Not to   mention that there were other big NOR  competitors like Spansion and Samsung. So Numonyx looked to Phase Change  Memory as the company's potential   breakout product. PCM had the  attributes of both NOR and NAND:   mass storage and fast random access.  So it can conceivably replace both. In February 2008, before the spinout, Intel  announced that it had delivered the market's first   PCM prototypes, a device codenamed Alverstone - a  128-megabit memory fabbed on a 90-nanometer node. In the press release, Ed Doller,  Numonyx's future CTO said: > This is the most significant non-volatile  memory advancement in 40 years ... There   have been plenty of attempts to find and  develop new non-volatile memory technologies > Yet of all the concepts, PCM provides  the most compelling solution – and Intel   and STMicroelectronics are delivering  PCM into the hands of customers today. ## Storage Class Memories Numonyx was not alone. In the late 2000s,   it seemed like every memory  company was working on PCM. In 2008, IBM showed PCM research with memory  cells as small as 3 nanometers by 20 nanometers.   They called it a promising candidate for  a category called "storage-class memory". SCM is a perceived market niche  to be filled by a memory with the   traits of both hard disk drives and solid  state memories. Namely, a non-volatile,   solid state memory with hard-drive-like  cost-per-bit numbers and DRAM-like access times. Such memories would not be used for PCs,   but rather mobile phones and data centers.  Mobile phones, because non-volatility   saves on precious battery. But fast random  access and write times beats NOR and NAND. This also applies to data centers,   which buy DRAM because they want certain data  at hand for certain data-heavy applications   where HDDs are too slow - paying a space  and power consumption cost in doing so. The SCM concept blurs the line between  data storage memory and working memory.   And what IBM seemed to say in 2008 was that  they thought PCM could handle that job. Computer architects envisioned yet far  greater markets for PCM. One highly   cited paper published in 2009 by Microsoft  and Carnegie Mellon researchers proposed a   potential computer architecture that positioned  PCM as a DRAM replacement. Vibes were good. ## PCM in Mobile PCM's market entry strategy  targeted the mobile market. Why mobile? The product had a natural target: NOR  flash memory that stored critical program code.   PCM can do that - enabling instant-on performance  for such devices - and store data too. At the same time, mobile was booming.  PCM's weakness was that it cost far   more than NAND. Mobile's volumes  can cut those costs. So Samsung,   Micron and others positioned PCM  as a low-power memory for wireless. So rather than getting NOR for the  boot code, flash for mass storage,   and DRAM for working memory, vendors can just get  PCM and DRAM together. Or if that is not feasible,   swap in PCM for frequently accessed  NAND-stored items like SQL databases. And it kinda had a chance at the time because the  NAND industry was switching from single-level to   multi-level NAND cells. The former stores one  bit per cell, while the latter 2 or more. But   the higher capacity was counterbalanced by meh  performance. It was maybe a window for PCM. In 2009, Samsung announced availability  of a 512 megabit PCM, calling it PRAM. Produced at a 60 nanometer node, they said  that PRAM - when paired with DRAM - can   offer over 20% power consumption  savings over DRAM-only offerings. Sei-Jin Kim, vice president of  the mobile memory planning and   enabling group in the Memory Division  at Samsung Electronics told the press   that PRAM is expected to become a  core memory product in the future. Numonyx showed their own PCM research  prototypes - done in concert with   Intel - in 2009, and targeted  a 1-gigabit PCM by end of 2010. Then in February 2010, Micron announced  the acquisition of Numonyx for ~$1.2   billion in stock, inheriting its  PCM technology. In July 2012,   Micron finally released the 1-gigabit PCM, a  mobile product fabbed on the 45 nanometer node. When paired with a 512-megabit  standard DRAM memory, there was   just enough to power certain feature phones. Nokia put it into their Asha handsets in late   2012. Smartphones and tablets  were on the future roadmap. But this momentum ended in August 2013 when  Samsung announced mass production of a scalable   24-layer 3D NAND. The subsequent literal rise  of 3D NAND sparked the greatest cost-per-bit   scaling curve in semiconductor history and ended  the most compelling reason to try mobile PCM. In January 2014, Micron said that it was  pulling its mobile PCM from the market after   a strategic evaluation. Vendors had spoken, they  preferred NAND and DRAM over NAND, DRAM, and PCM. But the company was not giving  up. At the 2014 announcement,   Micron hinted at a future product  with better cost-per-bit and power   consumption. A year later in 2015, Micron  and Intel together introduced 3D XPoint. ## 3D XPoint The two silicon giants positioned  3D XPoint between NAND and DRAM. It would be fast like DRAM  but nonvolatile like NAND.   And it can be what IBM said data centers  would need from storage class memories:   Fast access to a lot of data  without buying expensive DRAM. Mark Adams, Micron's president said: > "One of the most significant hurdles in modern  computing is the time it takes the processor to   reach data on long-term storage. This new class of  non-volatile memory is a revolutionary technology   that allows for quick access to enormous data  sets and enables entirely new applications." Weirdly enough, Intel and Micron declined to  say what 3D XPoint actually was - just saying   that it relies on a "bulk material property  change" and resistance but it was not a ReRAM. But you know, the Internet is full of sleuths  and a quick patent search pointed to phase change   memory. I suppose the secrecy was due to PCM's  pre-existing negative history setting a bias. Anyway, 3D XPoint just described the base  technology. Intel and Micron planned to   build their own brands with it. Micron's  version was called QuantX. Intel's was Optane. ## QuantX Micron targeted QuantX at data centers. In August  2016, they painted a rosy picture of its future. On a per-gigabyte basis, QuantX was priced  at half that of DRAM but 4-5 times of NAND.   The idea being that data centers can tear  out their DRAM and augment their NAND. Jon Carter (of Mars) said that the  first generation of QuantX SSDs   would be out in Q2 2017 and that demand  was very robust. He told ComputerWorld: > The issue I have right now ... is not about the  ability for revenue. We’ve built the capacity for   the first couple of years; it’s all accounted for.  I’ve been in situations with partners who buy a   lot of DRAM who’ve said, ‘Do you know how much  DRAM I buy? You’d better get me some 3D XPoint.’ > The demand is through the roof. There’s  not enough. We’re trying to manage the   capacity and the capital expense to build  the capacity for years three, four and five. > I’ve had a long line of all the major  storage and server vendors out there…   coming to me directly talking about  how they can get access to 3D XPoint Sadly the release slipped. A little delay  is probably to be expected considering it   is a brand new technology. But two  years passed from the 2016 hype,   and Micron still had not yet released  a 3D XPoint SSD or DRAM replacement. In July 2018, Intel and Micron agreed on  an amicable split. They will finish joint   development of the second generation of 3D  XPoint and then work independently after that. The split probably had to do with  disagreement on where to take the   product. Intel initially targeted its  Optane SSDs at consumer PCs and laptops,   likely because they wanted volume  sales to drive down wafer costs. Micron on the other hand wanted to go  to the data center right off the bat.   The aforementioned Jon Carter  hinted at this in 2016,   saying that consumer systems don't really  need 3D XPoint's strengths in low latency,   non-volatility and endurance. At least, not  enough to pay 4-5 times the NAND price for it. This split was cemented in October 2018 when  Micron announced that it will pay $1.5 billion   to buy out Intel's half of the Utah-based  semiconductor fab that the two companies   had shared to make XPoint. Intel would in-house  the manufacturing for their own XPoint products. On the earnings call, Micron CFO  Dave Zinsner said that the two had   invested $6 billion in total on this  fab, called IM Flash Technologies. A year later, they unveiled their first SSD  product: The Micron X100 SSD. Its technicals   were exceptional: 9+ gigabytes per second  bandwidth and eight microsecond latency.   But it was a storage device like  NAND, not a working memory like DRAM. ## Optane The first Optane product was released in 2017:  a 16 or 32-gigabyte PC accelerator module. It worked with Intel's latest CPUs  and motherboards to give computers   with HDDs SSD-like performance. Intel  claimed PC boot times cut in half,   28% overall faster performance,  and 65% faster game loading times. Reviewers took pains to emphasize that  Optane does not replace DRAM or NAND,   but augments it so users get reduced  wait times and faster task completion. While it did do that, the boost was not as  big as what the "1000x" headlines implied.   Real-world tests concluded that  the improvements depended on the   specific game or application. And  even then, they were not drastic. Analysts have speculated that this perhaps  was because it used industry-standard block   storage-oriented nonvolatile memory  express (NVMe) software interface   and PCIe bus standards which imposed  external bottlenecks on performance. Reviewers mostly concluded that it was a cool  technology that actually worked - which is more   than what you can say for a lot of things.  However its appeal was niche and end users   were confused on when it might actually be  of use. Where was Intel going with this? ## Going to the Data Center Intel's Optane strategy was to make it a critical  part of a larger "Intel" compute platform. They were aware that bottlenecks in  moving memory in and out of their Xeon   CPUs imposed major restrictions on  performance. They did not make DRAM,   but they did make NAND. Both  aren’t going to fix the bottleneck. So let's bring in this new memory Optane that  can work in tandem with those Xeons and 3D   NAND to open a major - and proprietary  - performance lead over competitors. As listed in a February 2017 investor  presentation, NAND would be "warm data",   lower cost and higher density, while Optane  can handle the higher performance "hot data". And since they were Intel - home  of Moore's Law - they can leverage   their manufacturing prowess to drive down cost. Intel executive Shannon Poulin in a  2018 interview laid out the thinking: > The ability to put an entire set  of analytics or an entire database   into memory delivers you just  massive performance improvement,   because then I don't need to go through the  interface, from the CPU to the hard drive > It's not just the SSD and the HDD  comparison ... It's non-volatile   memory connected directly  to the CPU, replacing DRAM,   which is a completely different paradigm. And  we felt like we could do it cost-effectively. Recall in 2017 that Intel released its  aforementioned PC accelerator. Poulin   explained that Intel chose to release this  accelerator module for client PCs - plus   an SSD - because it was easier to bring  to the market since the bus and software   standards were already there - and  their volumes can help fill the fab. Though as I mentioned, while those  standards got things faster to market,   they also apparently chained up  the technology's full strengths. But the strategy would find its real footing  when Intel released Optane in a DIMM form factor   that can slot into data center circuit boards.  This is an opportunity that Poulin said could   be worth billions. This would be the battlefield  that decides whether or not Optane has a future. ## The Data Center Optane's path to the data center was complicated. With the SSDs and PC accelerator  modules, Optane can slot in and act   as like a faster storage-type memory  - like NAND - with minimal problems. But if we want to use Optane as a working memory  like DRAM - the larger market opportunity - that   requires new circuit board designs and  cooperation with software providers. The first DIMMs - dubbed Optane DC Persistent  Memory - entered the market in April 2019,   four years after the XPoint announcement.  And as expected, it required a lot of   customization - including a compatible  Xeon processor, chipset, and motherboard. Then there’s the developers. Intel  signed deals with major partners   to integrate their data-intense applications. But   Optane's complexity made programming  software for it somewhat difficult. There were two modes. One was a "Memory Mode"  that turned Optane and DRAM together into a   pool of volatile memory. The DRAM caches  the most widely accessed data and Optane   just extends that. This works out-of-the-box,  but as ServeTheHome pointed out at the time,   Optane's value here is relative  to DRAM's fluctuating prices. The other mode is App Direct Mode,  which is where the real deal value   is. If a software supports it,  then they can write persistent   data to Optane memory modules like as  if it were an extraordinarily fast SSD. Normally, if an Oracle or SAP database does  a restart, it has to reload data into the   working DRAM from the SSDs or Hard Drives. For  big databases, this can take an hour or more.   But with Optane, that data remains after  a power cycle and can be accessed super   fast. One not-exact-but-directional  test cited a 12.5x improvement. This is why Oracle and SAP signed on.  Supporting persistent memory can help   the experience of recovering from a failure  - though it doesn't entirely remove the need   for proper backups and replication.  But App Direct Mode is a strange thing   that requires programmers to rewire their  thinking about data and data consistency. A year later in 2020, Intel gave  people an update on Optane adoption,   citing 582 proofs of concepts in their pipeline.   High-performance database applications like SAP  HANA and Oracle Exadata were prominent users. Most the other PoCs used Optane for various  high performance compute tasks, infrastructure,   and some AI/analytics. And just 40% used  Optane's more useful App Direct Mode. Intel   said they felt the industry will eventually  adopt this mode, but it could take years. Intel evidently expected people to  use persistent memory for virtual   infrastructure since one of its benefits is  allowing for more virtual machine instances   or memory per existing instance. But  most of the internal use cases by cloud   providers involved real-time video or shopping  recommendations - which sounds like an AI thing. Around the same time, Intel announced  that it would sell its 3D NAND business   to SK hynix, the Korean chipmaker, for $9 billion. Optane was not included in that transaction  - a seeming endorsement - but it did allow   people to back out an estimate of the product's  performance: a $500+ million implied loss in 2020. ## Micron Crashes Out In March 2021, Micron announced that it would  immediately cease development on 3D XPoint. Micron said that their Utah fab was consistently  under-utilized and it was costing the company   a run rate of $400 million a year. It  would later be sold to Texas Instruments. As to why 3D XPoint adoption  lagged, Micron management cited   ever-falling 3D NAND prices as well as  the difficult changes that data centers   and their applications must make in order  to make the full best use of the product. So instead, Micron said that they  would throw their weight behind an   open-standard interface technology  called Compute Express Link or CXL. CXL's promise is to connect together compute,   memory and storage systems into a pool that can  then be assigned to individual chips as needed. The original idea behind XPoint and Optane  was that getting data to the CPU was the   core bottleneck. But growth in machine  learning systems convinced Micron that it   was not just CPUs that needed more memory,  but also GPUs and AI accelerator ASICs. CXL can scratch that itch. But there were  also other DRAM-ish products that can too,   like High Bandwidth Memory. Optane  was just not the thing for the time. ## End The Micron news was not a major surprise.  After all, the company announced the X100   and then sort of forgot about it like  how Dany forgot about the Iron Fleet. But official confirmation of Micron's departure  greatly diminished the product. Without them,   customers can only rely on Intel for  supply - and single-sourcing makes   people nervous. Optane being a proprietary  memory technology did not help much either. And I think Micron so publicly flipping the   table spoiled Intel's years-long quiet  work in ecosystem-building. Moreover,   DRAM and especially 3D NAND swept the  table in terms of performance and cost. They not only got staggeringly cheaper,   but also cut their latencies against other  semiconductor memories. 3D NAND ate the   memory world - crushing the brief niche  opportunity that Optane wanted to fill. Intel’s Q2 2022 earnings call in July 2022 was  a pretty terrible earnings call overall. Intel   turned a net loss and revenue dropped 22% year  over year. Amidst that cavalcade of bad news,   Intel quietly announced that they  will wind down the Optane business. Products scheduled for release soon  afterwards like Optane Persistent   Memory 300 Series (Crow Pass) were  cancelled. Support for the Optane   portfolio of products entered End  of Life throughout 2024 and 2025. ## Conclusion Optane's failure stands as an  example of just how difficult   it can be to create a new memory category. Even flash took some two decades to build its  ecosystem, drive adoption at the consumer level,   and really hit its stride. While the modern  revival of PCM starts in 1999, 3D XPoint was   only announced in 2015. Products did not hit until  2017 and 2019, and it was in wind-down by 2022. The timing was wrong. 3D NAND scaled and  improved like nothing else in semiconductor   history. DRAMs got cheaper. AI wasn't  the monster that it is today (though I   am not sure whether Optane's CPU-centric  niche would have benefitted as much). There lingers some nostalgic wistfulness about  Optane. Considering how expensive DRAM is right   now, customers might now appreciate  an alternative like Optane. But the   product died for a reason. Jack  of all trades. Winner of none.

they partnered with Ovshinsky's Energy  Conversion Devices to start Ovonyx.
In February 2000, Ovonyx received a  big investment from Intel Capital,
as well as a licensing agreement. Then in 2001,  Intel started hyping Ovonic Unified Memory or OUM.
Made with a 180 nanometer node, the OUM generated  heat with a resistor to do SET and RESET and had
a bipolar junction transistor to access data.  According to Lowrey, all you needed to do to
make it was to add a layer of the chalcogenide  material on top of a normal silicon semiconductor.
Why was Intel so interested? At the  time, Intel was a dominant seller of
NOR flash - an older version of flash memory.  But NOR was hitting limits in scaling. The
memory cells had gotten so small that they  could no longer easily hold the charge.
Intel presented OUM as a potential next step that
can replace only just flash  but also maybe DRAM and SRAM.
The OUM product was then still in an  early research stage. It needed exotic,
expensive materials like tellurium, which drove up
the cost. And the strong currents needed  for SET and RESET were still rather large.
However, Chipzilla's backing and  marketing muscle sparked renewed
interest in phase change memory in  both industry and academia. Samsung
and STMicroelectronics licensed Ovonyx's  technology and started their own PCM efforts.
## Numonyx
In the end, the rise of another  type of flash memory called NAND
put the NOR flash business into secular decline.
NAND packs memory cells far more  densely than NOR does. And it
pushed back flash memory's perceived  scaling limits. Its cheap cost-per-bit
got it specced into items like the iPod  and smartphones - eating away at NOR.
In 2007, worldwide NOR flash sales fell 9%  year over year as NAND adoption by phones
accelerated. Continued declines  were expected in the years ahead.
NOR exposure was dragging down Intel's numbers.
In 2008, Intel completed its spin off of  its NOR flash business by merging it with
STMicroelectronics' flash business to form a  new Switzerland-based company called Numonyx.
Numonyx also received a cash injection from the  PE firm Francisco Partners as well as a bank loan.
So what was Numonyx going to do? The  NOR flash business was not the place
to be. NOR did not have NAND’s growth  prospects. NAND stores large pieces
of data and so had all the hard  disk drive storage market to eat.
NOR on the other hand was more suited  for fast random reads - so stuff like
operating system code for embedded  devices. Not a growth market. Not to
mention that there were other big NOR  competitors like Spansion and Samsung.
So Numonyx looked to Phase Change  Memory as the company's potential
breakout product. PCM had the  attributes of both NOR and NAND:
mass storage and fast random access.  So it can conceivably replace both.
In February 2008, before the spinout, Intel  announced that it had delivered the market's first
PCM prototypes, a device codenamed Alverstone - a  128-megabit memory fabbed on a 90-nanometer node.
In the press release, Ed Doller,  Numonyx's future CTO said:
> This is the most significant non-volatile  memory advancement in 40 years ... There
have been plenty of attempts to find and  develop new non-volatile memory technologies
> Yet of all the concepts, PCM provides  the most compelling solution – and Intel
and STMicroelectronics are delivering  PCM into the hands of customers today.
## Storage Class Memories
Numonyx was not alone. In the late 2000s,
it seemed like every memory  company was working on PCM.
In 2008, IBM showed PCM research with memory  cells as small as 3 nanometers by 20 nanometers.
They called it a promising candidate for  a category called "storage-class memory".
SCM is a perceived market niche  to be filled by a memory with the
traits of both hard disk drives and solid  state memories. Namely, a non-volatile,
solid state memory with hard-drive-like  cost-per-bit numbers and DRAM-like access times.
Such memories would not be used for PCs,
but rather mobile phones and data centers.  Mobile phones, because non-volatility
saves on precious battery. But fast random  access and write times beats NOR and NAND.
This also applies to data centers,
which buy DRAM because they want certain data  at hand for certain data-heavy applications
where HDDs are too slow - paying a space  and power consumption cost in doing so.
The SCM concept blurs the line between  data storage memory and working memory.
And what IBM seemed to say in 2008 was that  they thought PCM could handle that job.
Computer architects envisioned yet far  greater markets for PCM. One highly
cited paper published in 2009 by Microsoft  and Carnegie Mellon researchers proposed a
potential computer architecture that positioned  PCM as a DRAM replacement. Vibes were good.
## PCM in Mobile
PCM's market entry strategy  targeted the mobile market.
Why mobile? The product had a natural target: NOR  flash memory that stored critical program code.
PCM can do that - enabling instant-on performance  for such devices - and store data too.
At the same time, mobile was booming.  PCM's weakness was that it cost far
more than NAND. Mobile's volumes  can cut those costs. So Samsung,
Micron and others positioned PCM  as a low-power memory for wireless.
So rather than getting NOR for the  boot code, flash for mass storage,
and DRAM for working memory, vendors can just get  PCM and DRAM together. Or if that is not feasible,
swap in PCM for frequently accessed  NAND-stored items like SQL databases.
And it kinda had a chance at the time because the  NAND industry was switching from single-level to
multi-level NAND cells. The former stores one  bit per cell, while the latter 2 or more. But
the higher capacity was counterbalanced by meh  performance. It was maybe a window for PCM.
In 2009, Samsung announced availability  of a 512 megabit PCM, calling it PRAM.
Produced at a 60 nanometer node, they said  that PRAM - when paired with DRAM - can
offer over 20% power consumption  savings over DRAM-only offerings.
Sei-Jin Kim, vice president of  the mobile memory planning and
enabling group in the Memory Division  at Samsung Electronics told the press
that PRAM is expected to become a  core memory product in the future.
Numonyx showed their own PCM research  prototypes - done in concert with
Intel - in 2009, and targeted  a 1-gigabit PCM by end of 2010.
Then in February 2010, Micron announced  the acquisition of Numonyx for ~$1.2
billion in stock, inheriting its  PCM technology. In July 2012,
Micron finally released the 1-gigabit PCM, a  mobile product fabbed on the 45 nanometer node.
When paired with a 512-megabit  standard DRAM memory, there was
just enough to power certain feature phones.
Nokia put it into their Asha handsets in late
2012. Smartphones and tablets  were on the future roadmap.
But this momentum ended in August 2013 when  Samsung announced mass production of a scalable
24-layer 3D NAND. The subsequent literal rise  of 3D NAND sparked the greatest cost-per-bit
scaling curve in semiconductor history and ended  the most compelling reason to try mobile PCM.
In January 2014, Micron said that it was  pulling its mobile PCM from the market after
a strategic evaluation. Vendors had spoken, they  preferred NAND and DRAM over NAND, DRAM, and PCM.
But the company was not giving  up. At the 2014 announcement,
Micron hinted at a future product  with better cost-per-bit and power
consumption. A year later in 2015, Micron  and Intel together introduced 3D XPoint.
## 3D XPoint
The two silicon giants positioned  3D XPoint between NAND and DRAM.
It would be fast like DRAM  but nonvolatile like NAND.
And it can be what IBM said data centers  would need from storage class memories:
Fast access to a lot of data  without buying expensive DRAM.
Mark Adams, Micron's president said:
> "One of the most significant hurdles in modern  computing is the time it takes the processor to
reach data on long-term storage. This new class of  non-volatile memory is a revolutionary technology
that allows for quick access to enormous data  sets and enables entirely new applications."
Weirdly enough, Intel and Micron declined to  say what 3D XPoint actually was - just saying
that it relies on a "bulk material property  change" and resistance but it was not a ReRAM.
But you know, the Internet is full of sleuths  and a quick patent search pointed to phase change
memory. I suppose the secrecy was due to PCM's  pre-existing negative history setting a bias.
Anyway, 3D XPoint just described the base  technology. Intel and Micron planned to
build their own brands with it. Micron's  version was called QuantX. Intel's was Optane.
## QuantX
Micron targeted QuantX at data centers. In August  2016, they painted a rosy picture of its future.
On a per-gigabyte basis, QuantX was priced  at half that of DRAM but 4-5 times of NAND.
The idea being that data centers can tear  out their DRAM and augment their NAND.
Jon Carter (of Mars) said that the  first generation of QuantX SSDs
would be out in Q2 2017 and that demand  was very robust. He told ComputerWorld:
> The issue I have right now ... is not about the  ability for revenue. We’ve built the capacity for
the first couple of years; it’s all accounted for.  I’ve been in situations with partners who buy a
lot of DRAM who’ve said, ‘Do you know how much  DRAM I buy? You’d better get me some 3D XPoint.’
> The demand is through the roof. There’s  not enough. We’re trying to manage the
capacity and the capital expense to build  the capacity for years three, four and five.
> I’ve had a long line of all the major  storage and server vendors out there…
coming to me directly talking about  how they can get access to 3D XPoint
Sadly the release slipped. A little delay  is probably to be expected considering it
is a brand new technology. But two  years passed from the 2016 hype,
and Micron still had not yet released  a 3D XPoint SSD or DRAM replacement.
In July 2018, Intel and Micron agreed on  an amicable split. They will finish joint
development of the second generation of 3D  XPoint and then work independently after that.
The split probably had to do with  disagreement on where to take the
product. Intel initially targeted its  Optane SSDs at consumer PCs and laptops,
likely because they wanted volume  sales to drive down wafer costs.
Micron on the other hand wanted to go  to the data center right off the bat.
The aforementioned Jon Carter  hinted at this in 2016,
saying that consumer systems don't really  need 3D XPoint's strengths in low latency,
non-volatility and endurance. At least, not  enough to pay 4-5 times the NAND price for it.
This split was cemented in October 2018 when  Micron announced that it will pay $1.5 billion
to buy out Intel's half of the Utah-based  semiconductor fab that the two companies
had shared to make XPoint. Intel would in-house  the manufacturing for their own XPoint products.
On the earnings call, Micron CFO  Dave Zinsner said that the two had
invested $6 billion in total on this  fab, called IM Flash Technologies.
A year later, they unveiled their first SSD  product: The Micron X100 SSD. Its technicals
were exceptional: 9+ gigabytes per second  bandwidth and eight microsecond latency.
But it was a storage device like  NAND, not a working memory like DRAM.
## Optane
The first Optane product was released in 2017:  a 16 or 32-gigabyte PC accelerator module.
It worked with Intel's latest CPUs  and motherboards to give computers
with HDDs SSD-like performance. Intel  claimed PC boot times cut in half,
28% overall faster performance,  and 65% faster game loading times.
Reviewers took pains to emphasize that  Optane does not replace DRAM or NAND,
but augments it so users get reduced  wait times and faster task completion.
While it did do that, the boost was not as  big as what the "1000x" headlines implied.
Real-world tests concluded that  the improvements depended on the
specific game or application. And  even then, they were not drastic.
Analysts have speculated that this perhaps  was because it used industry-standard block
storage-oriented nonvolatile memory  express (NVMe) software interface
and PCIe bus standards which imposed  external bottlenecks on performance.
Reviewers mostly concluded that it was a cool  technology that actually worked - which is more
than what you can say for a lot of things.  However its appeal was niche and end users
were confused on when it might actually be  of use. Where was Intel going with this?
## Going to the Data Center
Intel's Optane strategy was to make it a critical  part of a larger "Intel" compute platform.
They were aware that bottlenecks in  moving memory in and out of their Xeon
CPUs imposed major restrictions on  performance. They did not make DRAM,
but they did make NAND. Both  aren’t going to fix the bottleneck.
So let's bring in this new memory Optane that  can work in tandem with those Xeons and 3D
NAND to open a major - and proprietary  - performance lead over competitors.
As listed in a February 2017 investor  presentation, NAND would be "warm data",
lower cost and higher density, while Optane  can handle the higher performance "hot data".
And since they were Intel - home  of Moore's Law - they can leverage
their manufacturing prowess to drive down cost.
Intel executive Shannon Poulin in a  2018 interview laid out the thinking:
> The ability to put an entire set  of analytics or an entire database
into memory delivers you just  massive performance improvement,
because then I don't need to go through the  interface, from the CPU to the hard drive
> It's not just the SSD and the HDD  comparison ... It's non-volatile
memory connected directly  to the CPU, replacing DRAM,
which is a completely different paradigm. And  we felt like we could do it cost-effectively.
Recall in 2017 that Intel released its  aforementioned PC accelerator. Poulin
explained that Intel chose to release this  accelerator module for client PCs - plus
an SSD - because it was easier to bring  to the market since the bus and software
standards were already there - and  their volumes can help fill the fab.
Though as I mentioned, while those  standards got things faster to market,
they also apparently chained up  the technology's full strengths.
But the strategy would find its real footing  when Intel released Optane in a DIMM form factor
that can slot into data center circuit boards.  This is an opportunity that Poulin said could
be worth billions. This would be the battlefield  that decides whether or not Optane has a future.
## The Data Center Optane's path to the data center was complicated.
With the SSDs and PC accelerator  modules, Optane can slot in and act
as like a faster storage-type memory  - like NAND - with minimal problems.
But if we want to use Optane as a working memory  like DRAM - the larger market opportunity - that
requires new circuit board designs and  cooperation with software providers.
The first DIMMs - dubbed Optane DC Persistent  Memory - entered the market in April 2019,
four years after the XPoint announcement.  And as expected, it required a lot of
customization - including a compatible  Xeon processor, chipset, and motherboard.
Then there’s the developers. Intel  signed deals with major partners
to integrate their data-intense applications. But
Optane's complexity made programming  software for it somewhat difficult.
There were two modes. One was a "Memory Mode"  that turned Optane and DRAM together into a
pool of volatile memory. The DRAM caches  the most widely accessed data and Optane
just extends that. This works out-of-the-box,  but as ServeTheHome pointed out at the time,
Optane's value here is relative  to DRAM's fluctuating prices.
The other mode is App Direct Mode,  which is where the real deal value
is. If a software supports it,  then they can write persistent
data to Optane memory modules like as  if it were an extraordinarily fast SSD.
Normally, if an Oracle or SAP database does  a restart, it has to reload data into the
working DRAM from the SSDs or Hard Drives. For  big databases, this can take an hour or more.
But with Optane, that data remains after  a power cycle and can be accessed super
fast. One not-exact-but-directional  test cited a 12.5x improvement.
This is why Oracle and SAP signed on.  Supporting persistent memory can help
the experience of recovering from a failure  - though it doesn't entirely remove the need
for proper backups and replication.  But App Direct Mode is a strange thing
that requires programmers to rewire their  thinking about data and data consistency.
A year later in 2020, Intel gave  people an update on Optane adoption,
citing 582 proofs of concepts in their pipeline.
High-performance database applications like SAP  HANA and Oracle Exadata were prominent users.
Most the other PoCs used Optane for various  high performance compute tasks, infrastructure,
and some AI/analytics. And just 40% used  Optane's more useful App Direct Mode. Intel
said they felt the industry will eventually  adopt this mode, but it could take years.
Intel evidently expected people to  use persistent memory for virtual
infrastructure since one of its benefits is  allowing for more virtual machine instances
or memory per existing instance. But  most of the internal use cases by cloud
providers involved real-time video or shopping  recommendations - which sounds like an AI thing.
Around the same time, Intel announced  that it would sell its 3D NAND business
to SK hynix, the Korean chipmaker, for $9 billion.
Optane was not included in that transaction  - a seeming endorsement - but it did allow
people to back out an estimate of the product's  performance: a $500+ million implied loss in 2020.
## Micron Crashes Out
In March 2021, Micron announced that it would  immediately cease development on 3D XPoint.
Micron said that their Utah fab was consistently  under-utilized and it was costing the company
a run rate of $400 million a year. It  would later be sold to Texas Instruments.
As to why 3D XPoint adoption  lagged, Micron management cited
ever-falling 3D NAND prices as well as  the difficult changes that data centers
and their applications must make in order  to make the full best use of the product.
So instead, Micron said that they  would throw their weight behind an
open-standard interface technology  called Compute Express Link or CXL.
CXL's promise is to connect together compute,
memory and storage systems into a pool that can  then be assigned to individual chips as needed.
The original idea behind XPoint and Optane  was that getting data to the CPU was the
core bottleneck. But growth in machine  learning systems convinced Micron that it
was not just CPUs that needed more memory,  but also GPUs and AI accelerator ASICs.
CXL can scratch that itch. But there were  also other DRAM-ish products that can too,
like High Bandwidth Memory. Optane  was just not the thing for the time.
## End
The Micron news was not a major surprise.  After all, the company announced the X100
and then sort of forgot about it like  how Dany forgot about the Iron Fleet.
But official confirmation of Micron's departure  greatly diminished the product. Without them,
customers can only rely on Intel for  supply - and single-sourcing makes
people nervous. Optane being a proprietary  memory technology did not help much either.
And I think Micron so publicly flipping the
table spoiled Intel's years-long quiet  work in ecosystem-building. Moreover,
DRAM and especially 3D NAND swept the  table in terms of performance and cost.
They not only got staggeringly cheaper,
but also cut their latencies against other  semiconductor memories. 3D NAND ate the
memory world - crushing the brief niche  opportunity that Optane wanted to fill.
Intel’s Q2 2022 earnings call in July 2022 was  a pretty terrible earnings call overall. Intel
turned a net loss and revenue dropped 22% year  over year. Amidst that cavalcade of bad news,
Intel quietly announced that they  will wind down the Optane business.
Products scheduled for release soon  afterwards like Optane Persistent
Memory 300 Series (Crow Pass) were  cancelled. Support for the Optane
portfolio of products entered End  of Life throughout 2024 and 2025.
## Conclusion
Optane's failure stands as an  example of just how difficult
it can be to create a new memory category.
Even flash took some two decades to build its  ecosystem, drive adoption at the consumer level,
and really hit its stride. While the modern  revival of PCM starts in 1999, 3D XPoint was
only announced in 2015. Products did not hit until  2017 and 2019, and it was in wind-down by 2022.
The timing was wrong. 3D NAND scaled and  improved like nothing else in semiconductor
history. DRAMs got cheaper. AI wasn't  the monster that it is today (though I
am not sure whether Optane's CPU-centric  niche would have benefitted as much).
There lingers some nostalgic wistfulness about  Optane. Considering how expensive DRAM is right
now, customers might now appreciate  an alternative like Optane. But the
product died for a reason. Jack  of all trades. Winner of none.
